faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Woodbury homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Woodbury host summer colonies, and in Gloucester County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Woodbury?
faqs.a: Woodbury sits in southwestern New Jersey across from Philadelphia, between the suburbs and the farm belt, and the habitat in between the houses — Scotland Run Park — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

Groundhogs burrow under sheds and decks across the farm-edge subdivisions of Washington Township, Monroe and Harrison, squirrels and raccoons fill attics in Deptford and Woodbury's older stock, and moles work the big new-subdivision lawns in Mantua and Woolwich — and Woodbury is squarely part of that pattern, with raccoons and gray squirrels in attics, skunks and opossums under decks, and seasonal bat work in the older rooflines.

Woodbury and Glassboro keep older Victorian and colonial cores, Deptford and Washington Township are postwar and growth-era subdivisions, and the south stays farmhouses and rural homes on large lots. In fall and winter, squirrels and rodents push into warm attics and wall voids in Woodbury; spring brings denning raccoons and groundhog and skunk activity in yards, and summer is bat and mole season. Most Woodbury jobs start with a full roofline and foundation inspection, then removal and sealing of every entry we find, because closing only the obvious hole rarely holds.

faqs.q: Why can't I get an exact wildlife quote for my Deptford Township home over the phone?
faqs.a: Because the same scratching sound can mean a short fix or a colony that has been overhead for two seasons — nobody honest can price it from a description. An Almonesson split-level with skunks under the slab-side porch and an Oak Valley ranch with squirrels in the eaves are both weekly Deptford calls, and neither can be priced honestly from a doorstep description. After the inspection you hold a written figure covering removal, entry sealing, and cleanup, and the work does not begin until you approve it.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Deptford Township lawn at night and it smells like skunk — what is going on?
faqs.a: Neat, cone-shaped holes in turf mean a skunk is mining grubs and earthworms, and late winter adds mating-season scent to the picture. The creek-corridor lawns in Deptford are grub country, and the skunk digging often shows up the same week the lawn service treats, which tells you the food, not the skunk, arrived first. The lasting answer is removing the den site and the food: we clear any skunk sheltering under steps or sheds, screen those voids, and talk through grub-heavy turf, because a lawn full of larvae gets visited nightly no matter how many skunks are taken off it.

Deptford Township.wildlife_intro:
Deptford is one of Gloucester County's older suburbs: postwar neighborhoods in Almonesson and Oak Valley, village pockets like Jericho, and commercial strips along Routes 41, 42, and 47 with housing tucked behind all of it. The Big Timber Creek branches and the township's many wooded stream corridors thread the subdivisions. Squirrels and raccoons work the mature-canopy streets, groundhogs dig the creek banks and the lots that back onto them, skunks work the lawns, and the older blocks near the commercial corridors add rats around dumpsters and rear yards.

Food decides where animals settle. Bird feeders spill seed that feeds rats at night, pet dishes sit out on porches, trash waits in cans a raccoon can open in seconds, and fallen fruit ferments under backyard trees. Removal without changing that menu is a short truce. We go over the property's food map with the homeowner — secured cans, feeders on baffled poles set away from the house, fruit picked up, grills cleaned — because the houses that stay quiet are the ones that stop advertising. The animal work and the housekeeping have to happen together. Deptford's corridor blocks need the food conversation as much as the sealing, and the plan for those streets names the dumpster and alley fixes alongside the house work.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Washington Township garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. At the township's farm edges the garden raids commute from burrows in the field line behind the subdivision fences, so the plan treats the burrow at the lot's rear, not just the fence the animal climbs. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

faqs.q: Can you get a raccoon family out of a Washington Township chimney?
faqs.a: Yes, and spring families are handled as families. A mother raccoon picks an uncapped flue because it mimics a hollow tree, and pups too young to climb are never sealed in or left behind — we check the flue first, reunite or remove the litter with the mother, and fit a proper cap once the chimney is empty. Whitman Square's chimneys are hitting the age where caps rust through together, and a spring litter here usually means the cap failed two winters ago. Raccoons are a New Jersey rabies-vector species, so the work is done with that caution built in.

Washington Township.wildlife_intro:
Washington Township, the Gloucester County one anchored by Turnersville, is a big, fast-grown suburb: Whitman Square and dozens of other subdivisions along the Black Horse Pike and Hurffville Road, Grenloch's older lake community, and farm remnants at the edges. The subdivisions are old enough now for mature trees and tired soffits, and the calls follow. Squirrels and raccoons in the colonials, groundhogs along the farm and field edges, skunks under the decks, and bats in the quieter attics out toward the township's rural south end.

Most entries are not holes animals made — they are building failures animals found. Fascia boards rot behind gutters, soffit panels sag at the seams, and a gray squirrel needs only a small gap and one afternoon to widen it. Repairs here mean replacing the rotted wood, not just covering it, then backing vents and eave returns with metal that teeth cannot work through. Paint-matched covers keep the fix invisible from the street. Gutters clogged with leaf litter matter too: standing water softens the very boards that are supposed to keep animals out. Washington Township's 1980s and 1990s colonials are hitting the age where every original soffit and vent is a candidate entry, and the inspection here treats the whole run, not the one hole reported.

faqs.q: I found bat droppings in my Glassboro attic — what happens next?
faqs.a: First we confirm the colony's size and find every entry, which is usually a cluster of small gaps at the ridge, a gable vent, or lifted flashing rather than one obvious hole. A Glassboro rental attic can hold a colony for several seasons before a tenant reports the smell, and those late discoveries are exactly the jobs where the cleanup conversation needs photographs. Exclusion happens inside the NJ Fish & Wildlife guideline windows — April 1 to May 14 or August 1 to October 15 — using one-way exits, and the guano cleanup afterward is handled as a health material, bagged out rather than swept into the air.

faqs.q: Why do I hear running in my Glassboro ceiling every morning?
faqs.a: Daytime running, especially at dawn and mid-afternoon, points to gray squirrels — they commute. Near campus the morning running usually belongs to squirrels commuting between street trees and the converted houses' eave returns, and sealing one house on a rental block often starts a conversation with the whole block. A squirrel entry is usually a gnawed widening at a gable vent, dormer cheek, or eave return, and the repair has to replace the chewed wood and back it with metal, or the next squirrel reopens it in days. One-way doors let the animals leave on their own schedule; then the opening is closed for good.

Glassboro.wildlife_intro:
Glassboro is a college borough: Rowan University fills the center, student rentals fill the older streets around it, and family neighborhoods spread out past the campus edges. The rental stock, much of it older homes converted years ago, is where the wildlife work concentrates: squirrels in the eaves, bats in the attics nobody enters, raccoons in the chimneys. The family streets add groundhogs and skunks, and the township edges toward Scotland Run bring wooded lots with the full rural rotation.

The attic is where most of the damage hides. Droppings foul insulation until it stops insulating, urine soaks ceiling drywall, and nesting shreds stored boxes and wiring jackets. A proper attic job pairs the removal itself with a cleanup decision — spot-cleaning a light mess, or pulling and replacing badly fouled insulation once the animals are out and the entries are sealed. Bat guano gets handled as a health material, bagged and carried out rather than swept dry. Homeowners see photographs of what we found, so the cleanup scope is a choice, not a surprise. Glassboro's converted rentals often have attics no tenant has opened in years, so the documentation, photographs, entries, and colony evidence, is written for an owner who may manage the house from another county.

faqs.q: What makes one Williamstown wildlife job cost more than another?
faqs.a: Access, animal count, and aftermath. A steep roof, a maternity litter that has to be handled as a family, or insulation contaminated wall-to-wall all add time and material. A Victory Lakes cottage with a winter raccoon tenancy and a Main Street twin with one squirrel entry price very differently, and the access-and-aftermath breakdown in the quote is what shows the owner why. The inspection sorts your house into one of those buckets and the written quote shows exactly which items drive the number.

faqs.q: A groundhog is burrowing under my Williamstown foundation — how bad is that?
faqs.a: Worse than it looks. A groundhog burrow system runs many feet with several chambers, and soil removed from under a slab or footing leaves voids that crack concrete and channel water against the foundation. In the sandy ground past the Pike, a Williamstown groundhog can undermine a whole shed floor in a season; the fans of pale sand at the entrances are the giveaway residents should report early. We trap at the active entrances, then backfill and screen the site so the next groundhog inherits a closed burrow. Groundhogs are on New Jersey's rabies-vector list — one more reason not to corner one yourself.

Williamstown.wildlife_intro:
Williamstown is Monroe Township's downtown: an older Main Street and Black Horse Pike core of small homes and twins, Victory Lakes' cottage community, and a long rural tail running southeast into the pines toward Winslow. The mix produces two call logs in one town. In the core: raccoons, squirrels, and rats around the older blocks. At the lakes and the rural tail: groundhogs in the sandy soil, skunks under cabins, bats in quiet attics, and Barrens-edge snakes in the woodpiles.

Empty houses invite quiet tenants. A home closed for the winter gives raccoons and bats months of undisturbed tenure, and the damage is usually discovered in a single bad hour at spring opening: fouled insulation, stained ceilings, a chimney full of nesting. Pre-closing walk-throughs in the fall — caps checked, vents screened, gaps at the waterline and roofline sealed — cost far less than post-winter remediation. For owners who are away, a neighbor or caretaker holding a key is the next best thing; small leaks and small entries both grow in an empty house. Victory Lakes' cottages sit empty in stretches like shore houses do, so Williamstown's fall closing check covers the lake streets as well as the year-round core.

faqs.q: I can hear baby animals in my Mantua Township wall — can you just seal the hole?
faqs.a: Not yet, and any company offering to should worry you. Sealing a mother out with a litter inside converts a removal into dead animals in the wall. In Mantua's village chimneys the spring litters are usually announced by flies at the flue in May, which means the family has been in residence since March, and the flue gets a camera check before anything is discussed. We locate the litter first, then time the work so the family leaves or is taken out together — one-way exits sized for the species, or hands-on removal where the young cannot climb. The hole gets sealed the same visit the last animal is confirmed out, not before.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Mantua Township deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. Creek-side Mantua gives opossums everything they want, water, cover, and low decks, and most calls end with a screened deck and a compost bin moved, not just an animal removed. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

Mantua Township.wildlife_intro:
Mantua is a township of villages and creek ground: the old Mantua village center, Barnsboro's crossroads homes, and postwar subdivisions spreading toward Wenonah and the Richwood farmland. Mantua Creek and its tributaries cut through the middle, and the creek lots get the animals first. Raccoons commute up from the creek to the chimneys, groundhogs dig the banks and the gardens behind them, skunks work the low ground, and squirrels and bats take the older village houses. The farm edges add barn-loft raccoons and outbuilding skunks.

Decks and porches fail at ground level. The gap beneath a low deck is dark, dry, and sheltered enough for skunks, opossums, and groundhogs to den in, and lattice alone stops none of them. Lasting work means trenching around the structure and burying galvanized hardware cloth in an L-shape, so an animal digging at the edge meets mesh angled outward underground. Lattice or skirting goes back over the top for looks. It is unglamorous digging, and it is the difference between a den that stays empty and one that fills again every spring. Mantua's creek-side decks are built low over damp ground, and that void is the township's most reliable den site, so deck screening leads most quotes here.
